extracted.intended_audience: registered public companies (registrants), their legal and accounting/advisory providers, auditors/attestation providers, and investors
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and explanatory guidance implementing the Commission's final climate-related (subpart 1500) disclosure requirements, including when and what GHG emissions and assurance/attestation information registrants must disclose and related safe-harbor and liability rules. Focused on disclosure, attestation/assurance procedures, oversight, and forward-looking safe harbors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of dismissal/resignation of attestation provider
rubrics_metrics.description: Registrant must provide disclosure where: (1) a GHG emissions attestation provider resigns or is dismissed during the fiscal year covered by the attestation report but does not issue the attestation report; and (2) a GHG emissions attestation provider issues an opinion or conclusion on GHG emissions disclosure for the relevant fiscal year but is dismissed or resigns before the attestation report is filed. (See 17 CFR 229.1506(d)(2)(i).)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rules require disclosure in both scenarios to ensure investors are informed when an attestation provider is replaced or departs during the relevant reporting period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of changes in attestation provider
rubrics_metrics.description: Registrants should disclose changes in attestation provider (e.g., change of provider) as required by the rules and as discussed in the Proposing Release and commenter letters (CFA Institute noted it would not object to a requirement to disclose a change in attestation provider).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This disclosure helps investors track continuity and changes in who is providing assurance on GHG disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of circumstances likely to cause dismissal/disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Registrants may be required to disclose the 'most likely circumstances' for dismissal or disagreement between the registrant and the GHG emissions attestation provider and provide examples (commenter suggestion reflected in discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission noted examples were suggested by commenters (e.g., ERM CVS) — providing such information can increase transparency about potential conflicts or disputes with assurance providers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary assurance disclosure (Item 1506(e)) — general categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Item 1506(e) requires registrants that voluntarily disclose GHG emissions and voluntarily obtain assurance to disclose the general categories of information specified in the final rules about those assurance services, rather than, for example, the fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission decided not to require disclosure of voluntary assurance fees, focusing instead on categories of information that are most useful to investors (see 17 CFR 229.1506(e); discussion rejecting fee disclosure as unnecessary/burdensome).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether a third-party service is an assurance engagement (determinative for Item 1506(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: The key factor for determining whether disclosure is necessary under Item 1506(e) is whether the third-party services are designed to provide assurance (limited or reasonable), not merely the label 'verification' or 'validation'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites examples/definitions in ISO 14064-3 and attestation standards (PCAOB, AICPA, IAASB). Services labeled 'verification' could be assurance if designed to provide assurance; conversely, some engagements (e.g., agreed-upon procedures) are not designed to provide assurance and therefore may not trigger the disclosure requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between limited and reasonable assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Final rules and the Proposing Release distinguish limited assurance from reasonable assurance; limited assurance provides a reduced level of assurance while reasonable assurance provides a high (but not absolute) level of assurance on historical data and information (ISO 14064-3 definitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registrants (and assurance providers) should identify the level of assurance (limited vs reasonable) because investors may have different expectations about reliability and depth of procedures performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of engagements designed to provide assurance and applicable standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of engagements designed to provide assurance include PCAOB AT section 101; AICPA SSAE No. 21 AT-C sections 205 and 206 and AICPA SSAE No. 22 AT-C section 210; IAASB ISAE 3000 (Revised) and ISAE 3410; and Proposed ISSA 5000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These standards exemplify the types of assurance engagements the Commission considered; registrants and investors can look to these standards to understand the nature and scope of procedures and reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of engagements not designed to provide assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of engagements that are not designed to provide assurance include PCAOB AT section 201 Agreed-Upon Procedures engagements; AICPA SSAE No. 19 AT-C section 215 Agreed-Upon Procedures; and IAASB ISRS 4400 (Revised) Agreed-Upon Procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreed-upon procedures engagements result in reports of factual findings rather than assurance conclusions and therefore are treated differently for disclosure purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of oversight inspection programs for attestation providers
rubrics_metrics.description: Registrants must disclose whether the GHG emissions attestation provider is subject to an oversight inspection program (e.g., AICPA peer review program, PCAOB inspection program) as part of the information about assurance services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AICPA peer review program is an example that includes GHG attestation engagements within its scope; PCAOB inspections are jurisdictionally limited to audits of issuers and brokers/dealers and do not generally include attestation engagements for GHG disclosures, though the PCAOB is cited as another non-exhaustive example of oversight generally. Even oversight programs that do not directly inspect GHG attestation engagements can be informative about a provider's overall quality-control environment (see discussion of oversight and spillover effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and role of the AICPA Peer Review Program
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the AICPA Peer Review Program, AICPA member firms must have a peer review every three years against the AICPA Standards for Performing and Reporting on Peer Reviews; the AICPA peer review program can include GHG attestation engagements within its scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission cites the AICPA program as an example oversight inspection program that would fall within the scope of required disclosure; registrants should note whether their providers participate in such programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attestation requirement tied to registrant categories (AFs and LAFs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the final rules, only Accelerated Filers (AFs) and Large Accelerated Filers (LAFs) are required to disclose Scopes 1 and 2 emissions in certain circumstances, and these categories of registrants are also required to obtain an attestation report. Thus, there is no category required to disclose GHG emissions but not obtain attestation under the final rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This differs from the proposed rules, which would have required disclosure of Scopes 1 and 2 for all registrants but attestation only for AFs and LAFs; the final rules align disclosure and attestation requirements for those categories to avoid a gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence standards for assurance providers
rubrics_metrics.description: Assurance engagements and providers are discussed in the context of independence standards such as the PCAOB Ethics and Independence Rules and Standards; AICPA Code of Professional Conduct; and IESBA International Code of Ethics for Professional Accountants (including International Independence Standards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registrants should disclose whether providers are subject to recognized independence standards and whether any independence considerations might affect the assurance provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable assurance methodologies referenced
rubrics_metrics.description: Commission references assurance methodologies such as AICPA AT-C 205 (Assertion-Based Examination Engagements), AICPA AT-C 210 (Review Engagements), IAASB ISAE 3000 (Revised), and ISAE 3410 (Assurance Engagements on Greenhouse Gas Statements) as used in practice for GHG assurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methodologies provide frameworks for designing assurance procedures and reporting; registrants and providers may rely on them when designing or describing assurance engagements.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement to disclose voluntary assurance fees
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission decided not to require disclosure of fees associated with voluntary assurance or verification services, concluding fee disclosure would not be useful to investors and would impose burdens on registrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead, the final rules focus on the general categories of information about the assurance service that are most useful to investors (see discussion rejecting fee disclosure; reference to letter from CEMEX).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 436 amendment — limited liability for assurance providers under Section 11
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to Rule 436 clarify that assurance providers will not be liable to shareholders in actions under section 11 of the Securities Act to the extent the provider qualifies for the exception; but registrants and providers remain subject to other remedies such as section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies scope of potential securities-law liability but does not eliminate other avenues of enforcement or private suits under fraud provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fragmentation of assurance standards and investor confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission recognized that fragmentation in voluntary assurance standards (varying levels and scopes among providers) has diminished comparability and may cause investor confusion about what an assurance report signifies (e.g., limited vs reasonable assurance, scope).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final rules aim to reduce confusion by requiring disclosure of specific information about assurance services so investors can evaluate whether assurance enhanced reliability of GHG disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCAOB inspection jurisdiction limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCAOB's inspection jurisdiction is limited to audits of issuers and registered brokers and dealers and does not include attestation engagements for GHG emissions disclosure within its scope (15 U.S.C. 7214).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although PCAOB inspections do not usually cover GHG attestation, PCAOB oversight is discussed as an example of inspection programs generally and academic literature suggests PCAOB inspections can have spillover effects improving quality on non-inspected engagements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement not to file written consent of attestation provider as exhibit
rubrics_metrics.description: A registrant would not have to obtain and include the written consent of the GHG emissions attestation provider pursuant to 17 CFR 229.601(b)(23) (the Regulation S-K provision requiring a registrant to file a written consent of an expert as an exhibit) when incorporating an attestation report by reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies exhibit-filing obligations and reduces administrative burden associated with including an expert's written consent where an attestation report is incorporated by reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe harbor for forward-looking statements (Item 1507) — scope and exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Item 1507 adopts safe-harbor protection for forward-looking statements made in subpart 1500 disclosures (consistent with PSLRA), applying to issuers and, where specified, persons acting on behalf of issuers, outside reviewers retained by issuers making statements on issuers' behalf, and underwriters (with respect to issuer-provided information). However, specified statutory exclusions apply (e.g., IPO-related statements, certain investment company statements, going-private/tender-offer/beneficial-ownership report contexts) and certain items (e.g., consolidated financial statements) may be excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission noted commenters' requests for PSLRA-like protection for novel disclosures; Item 1507 describes the safe harbor's reach and limitations, including that the Commission is not using exemptive authority to extend the PSLRA safe harbors beyond statutory boundaries in certain contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe-harbor application to issuers not subject to Exchange Act reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Item 1507(a)(3) provides that the safe harbor will apply where an issuer, at the time the statement is made, is not subject to the reporting requirements of section 13(a) or section 15(d) of the Exchange Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies that safe-harbor protections can apply to forward-looking statements made by entities not otherwise subject to Exchange Act periodic reporting, per Item 1507(a)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions and limits on safe-harbor protection consistent with statute
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission is not using its exemptive authority to extend the PSLRA safe harbors to specified categories (e.g., certain 'bad actors', investment company registration-statement contexts, going-private/tender-offer/beneficial-ownership report situations) and reiterates statutory limitations in 15 U.S.C. 77z-2 and 78u-5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registrants should not assume Item 1507 provides PSLRA-like protection in contexts explicitly excluded by statute or by the Commission's stated limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward-looking examples likely covered by Item 1507/PSLRA
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of forward-looking statements that would likely be covered include statements of potential capital expenditures (Item 1502(e) transition plans), plans to transition operations or product mixes (Item 1502(d), Item 1504), projections of future economic performance (Item 1502(d), Item 1504, Item 303), and projections or estimates of future GHG emissions (Item 1504).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples illustrate common climate-related disclosures that should be treated as forward-looking and evaluated under the safe-harbor rules and related statutory exceptions or limitations.
